questions.question: A server CPU delivers roughly 1–2 TFLOP/s on matrix workloads while a modern ML accelerator delivers hundreds of TFLOP/s on the same workload class. What structural choice in the accelerator is primarily responsible for this orders-of-magnitude gap?
choices: The accelerator clocks several times faster, so every instruction completes in a fraction of the CPU's cycle time
The accelerator eliminates the DRAM interface, so arithmetic units never stall on memory traffic
The accelerator devotes the majority of its silicon to parallel arithmetic arrays rather than to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and large coherent cache hierarchies
The accelerator executes neural-network operations without any control logic or instruction fetch
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Accelerators win by reallocating transistor budget: the control-dominated silicon that makes CPUs flexible becomes dense arithmetic arrays optimized for regular data-parallel work. The clock-frequency explanation is wrong because modern GPUs and TPUs actually run at lower clock rates than server CPUs; the gap comes from throughput per cycle, not cycles per second. The claim about eliminating DRAM confuses a different problem: accelerators still fight the memory wall and require high-bandwidth memory hierarchies. The claim about eliminating all control logic misdescribes the hardware, which still requires instruction fetch and dispatch.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why domain-specific silicon achieves orders-of-magnitude higher throughput than general-purpose CPUs on matrix workloads.

questions.question: A team replaces a CPU with a GPU that runs the parallelizable compute portion of a pipeline $500\times$ faster. Preprocessing, data loading, and launch overhead still account for 20 percent of end-to-end wall clock. Compute the maximum end-to-end speedup achievable and explain which lever the team must pull next.
questions.answer: Amdahl's Law gives $1/(0.2 + 0.8/500) \approx 4.96\times$ end-to-end speedup; the ideal ceiling as GPU speed approaches infinity is $1/0.2 = 5.0\times$. The 20 percent serial fraction dominates once the parallel portion is accelerated enough. Buying a faster GPU yields diminishing returns: doubling GPU throughput from $500\times$ to $1000\times$ moves the speedup only to about $4.98\times$. The practical consequence is that the next optimization must attack the serial fraction itself—parallel data loaders, kernel-launch batching, host-to-device overlap—rather than shopping for a faster accelerator.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the Amdahl-bounded end-to-end speedup for an accelerated workload and justify why the next optimization target is the serial fraction.

questions.question: A serving team switches a model from FP32 to INT8 inference on hardware whose tensor units pack four INT8 multiplies into the silicon area of one FP32 multiply. Which description best matches hardware-software co-design as the chapter defines it?
choices: The precision change is a purely algorithmic optimization that would deliver the same speedup on any hardware whose instruction set supports INT8 operands
The change is a hardware-only optimization because the software pipeline is untouched above the matrix kernel
The change is neither algorithmic nor hardware co-design because INT8 only reduces memory footprint, not compute time
The algorithmic change (lower precision) pays off because the silicon was designed to exploit that change, coupling software representation and hardware execution
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Co-design means the algorithmic choice and the hardware path are jointly engineered: INT8 wins on this accelerator because four INT8 MACs fit in one FP32 MAC's area, not because INT8 is intrinsically faster in the abstract. The claim that any INT8-capable hardware delivers the same speedup ignores that emulated INT8 on FP32 units can be slower than native FP32; co-design is precisely the property that makes the hardware match the algorithm. The memory-only claim confuses one benefit (smaller footprint) with the deeper coupling that defines co-design.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a proposed optimization as hardware-software co-design by testing whether the silicon was engineered to exploit the algorithmic change.

questions.question: True or False: If two accelerators advertise identical peak FLOP/s and run the same trained model, they are guaranteed to deliver roughly equal realized throughput.
questions.answer: False. Advertised peak FLOP/s represents only the theoretical arithmetic ceiling. Realized throughput is bounded by the lower of the compute ceiling and what memory bandwidth can deliver. For operations where data transfer time exceeds compute time, performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than peak FLOP/s—so two accelerators with identical peak compute but different memory bandwidths will deliver substantially different realized throughput.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish peak-FLOP/s parity from realized-throughput parity using memory bandwidth constraints.

questions.question: A team profiles two kernels on the same accelerator. Kernel A moves 40 GB of weight and activation data while executing 4 TFLOPs of useful work; kernel B moves 2 GB while executing 6 TFLOPs. Kernel A's much lower ____ (defined as the ratio of floating-point operations to bytes of memory traffic) explains why it is limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute throughput, while kernel B is compute bound.
questions.answer: arithmetic intensity. Arithmetic intensity (measured in FLOP/byte) determines whether a workload is memory bound or compute bound: kernel A achieves 100 FLOP/byte and starves for memory bandwidth, whereas kernel B achieves 3,000 FLOP/byte and keeps the arithmetic units fully occupied.
questions.learning_objective: Infer the arithmetic-intensity metric from a pair of profile traces and apply it to predict whether a kernel is limited by compute or bandwidth.

questions.question: What recurring structural pattern best explains the specialization path from the Intel 8087 through GPUs to TPUs?
choices: A dominant computational bottleneck in each era made general-purpose processors inefficient, prompting a specialized unit that was later absorbed into mainstream silicon as the workload stabilized
Each generation became progressively more general-purpose to maximize software portability, so specialization is essentially a transitional phase
Clock-frequency scaling drove each transition, with specialization emerging only after the final frequency ceiling was reached
Each generation replaced memory hierarchies with larger on-chip arithmetic arrays so data movement stopped constraining performance
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The 8087 solved floating-point cost, GPUs solved graphics throughput, and TPUs solved ML data movement—each followed the same pattern: specialized unit emerges to attack the dominant bottleneck, then mainstream silicon absorbs the successful features. The clock-frequency story is historically inverted: most specialization momentum came after Dennard scaling stalled, not before. The claim of becoming progressively more general-purpose gets the arrow wrong: the trend is toward domain-specific specialization.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the bottleneck-then-specialization pattern that produced each wave of domain-specific hardware.

questions.question: Why did domain-specific architectures become structurally necessary (not merely attractive) after Moore's Law slowed and Dennard scaling ended?
choices: Model compute demand began growing slower than hardware supply, so architects had free transistor budget to devote to specialized units

Power-density and thermal limits produced dark silicon: architects could no longer power every transistor simultaneously, so dedicating powered transistors to narrow high-value workloads became the only way to keep performance scaling
CPUs lost the ability to execute floating-point arithmetic, forcing the workload onto dedicated accelerators
Programmers preferred fixed-function hardware because it simplified debugging and deployment pipelines
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Once power density limits meant not all transistors on a die could be powered simultaneously at maximum frequency (dark silicon), generic scaling stopped delivering performance; dedicating the powered subset to workloads that use them intensely became the only remaining path. The claim that demand slowed is the opposite of reality: ML demand grew at $4{-}10\times$ per year, far outpacing general hardware supply.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how dark silicon and the end of Dennard scaling forced the shift to domain-specific architecture.

questions.question: Explain why machine learning created an "integration bottleneck" rather than merely another arithmetic bottleneck, and why this distinction drives accelerator design choices.
questions.answer: ML workloads combine massive parallelism, predictable dataflow, and precision tolerance, so the binding constraint becomes keeping thousands of arithmetic units fed with weights and activations rather than adding more arithmetic units. A single DRAM access can cost $100{-}1000\times$ the energy of a multiply-accumulate, so a design that doubles MACs without improving locality spends more energy on data movement than on compute. The consequence is that modern accelerators prioritize on-chip scratchpads, operand reuse structures, and hierarchical memory staging—design choices that would be wasteful if arithmetic itself were the bottleneck.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why data movement rather than arithmetic throughput became the dominant design axis for ML accelerators.

questions.question: Order the following specialization waves by what each one made architecturally necessary for the next: (1) Domain-specific AI accelerators emerge to exploit ML's regular dataflow, (2) Floating-point coprocessors establish the pattern of offloading a dominant primitive, (3) Parallel graphics processors prove that thousands of lightweight arithmetic units can be managed coherently, (4) ML-specific units refine DSAs around systolic arrays and mixed precision.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (2) Floating-point coprocessors establish the pattern of offloading a dominant primitive, (3) Parallel graphics processors prove that thousands of lightweight arithmetic units can be managed coherently, (1) Domain-specific AI accelerators emerge to exploit ML's regular dataflow, (4) ML-specific units refine DSAs around systolic arrays and mixed precision. Each wave made the next possible: FPUs normalized the offload-a-primitive playbook; GPUs proved mass parallelism was manageable; that management experience enabled DSAs to target ML dataflow; mature DSA techniques in turn enabled tensor-core and systolic refinement. Swapping GPUs ahead of FPUs breaks the enabling chain—mass parallelism without an offload playbook had no economic path to market.
questions.learning_objective: Order the four specialization waves causally and explain why each era's lessons enabled the next.

questions.question: A startup profiles batch-1 inference for a 7-billion-parameter autoregressive model on an accelerator and observes 5–10 percent compute utilization. Which diagnosis best matches the section's analysis?
choices: The model is too parallel for the hardware, so the scheduler is oversupplying work to the arithmetic units and forcing them to stall
The accelerator lacks adequate branch-prediction hardware for the control flow of the decoder loop
Reduced-precision arithmetic is unavailable during inference, forcing FP64 execution on every kernel
Autoregressive token-by-token generation produces too little parallel work per step to saturate the accelerator's thousands of arithmetic lanes, and weight reads dominate per-token time
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. It names the two conditions the chapter identifies: insufficient parallel work per step plus weight-read dominance at batch 1. The claim that the model is too parallel is self-contradictory. The branch-prediction claim imports a CPU-centric concern that does not fit accelerators optimized around regular dataflow; the control flow of autoregressive decoding is trivial, but the per-token weight traffic is the actual bottleneck.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose why an ML accelerator remains severely underutilized on small-batch autoregressive inference.

rationale.difficulty_progression: Begins with primitive taxonomy classification, explores im2col algorithmic transformation, analyzes SFU hardware trade-offs, discriminates vector access patterns, and finishes with a concrete numerical MAC scaling problem.

questions.question: Which mapping of neural-network operations to accelerator compute primitives best matches the architectural taxonomy of this section?
choices: Dense projections map to special function units because matrix multiplication is transcendental; softmax maps to vector units; element-wise activations map to matrix units

Dense matrix multiplications and linear projections map to dedicated matrix units, element-wise activations and vector reductions map to vector units, and transcendental activations (like exp, sigmoid, and rsqrt) map to special function units
All neural-network operations map identically to scalar ALUs because modern accelerators eliminate structural specialization among primitives
Element-wise activations map to matrix units because they share multi-dimensional tensor shape; GEMM reductions map to special function units
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The section decomposes operations into three distinct primitives: matrix units for structured many-to-many transformations (GEMM, linear layers), vector units for element-wise operations and 1D reductions (ReLU, pooling, bias add), and special function units (SFUs) for transcendental and nonlinear computations (exp, sigmoid, tanh, rsqrt). The claim that dense projections map to SFUs confuses linear matrix math with transcendental functions. The claim that accelerators eliminate primitive specialization contradicts the entire premise of domain-specific functional blocks.
questions.learning_objective: Match common neural-network operation classes to the accelerator primitives (vector, matrix, special function) that execute them efficiently.

questions.question: Explain why transforming a convolution into a matrix multiplication via the im2col (image-to-column) technique is advantageous for hardware execution despite causing a large memory footprint amplification (e.g., $9\times$ for a $3\times 3$ filter).
questions.answer: The im2col transformation explicitly duplicates overlapping input receptive fields into the columns of a dense 2D matrix, trading memory capacity for regular data organization. This converts a complex 6D nested convolution loop into a standard General Matrix Multiply (GEMM), allowing the workload to execute directly on dedicated, highly optimized hardware matrix units that achieve maximum compute density and throughput. The memory amplification is an accepted trade-off because regular dense matrix hardware delivers orders-of-magnitude higher throughput than executing irregular sliding-window scalar loops.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the memory-versus-compute trade-off of the im2col technique and explain how it maps convolution to matrix hardware primitives.

questions.question: Why do transcendental activation functions (such as $\text{sigmoid}$, $\tanh$, and $\text{softmax}$ exponentials) require dedicated Special Function Units (SFUs) or hardware approximations rather than executing on standard ALU/vector MAC pipelines?
choices: Transcendental functions require multi-dimensional matrix multiplications that standard vector units cannot express
Standard ALUs cannot represent negative numbers, which are required for sigmoid and tanh outputs

Transcendental functions cannot be computed in a single MAC cycle and would otherwise expand into iterative series or dozens of scalar instructions, causing activation layers to become execution bottlenecks
Special function units eliminate the need for memory loads by generating output activations directly from model weights
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Transcendental functions like $\exp(x)$, $\log(x)$, and $\sqrt{x}$ require iterative Taylor/Chebyshev series, CORDIC algorithms, or polynomial expansions that take dozens of cycles on standard arithmetic pipelines. SFUs use dedicated lookup tables, interpolation circuits, and specialized approximation hardware to compute these functions in very few cycles, preventing nonlinear activation layers from bottlenecking the pipeline. The claim that standard ALUs cannot represent negative numbers is false. The claim about eliminating memory loads misdescribes the role of arithmetic units.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why transcendental operations require dedicated Special Function Units (SFUs) rather than general ALU pipelines.

questions.question: True or False: Vector gather and scatter operations achieve the same high hardware throughput as contiguous vector loads and stores on modern accelerators because both are executed by the vector processing unit.
questions.answer: False. Contiguous vector loads and stores transfer consecutive memory addresses in single, wide, coalesced memory transactions that saturate bus bandwidth. In contrast, gather (nonconsecutive reads) and scatter (nonconsecutive writes) access scattered memory locations, causing multiple separate memory transactions, cache line underutilization, and memory bank conflicts, which substantially lowers effective memory throughput.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish contiguous vector memory operations from gather/scatter operations in terms of memory efficiency and hardware throughput.

questions.question: A linear layer processes a batch of 32 samples, transforming 256 input features into 512 output neurons. What is the total number of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations required for this forward pass, and which compute primitive executes the bulk of this work?
choices: $4{,}194{,}304$ MACs ($32 \times 256 \times 512$), executed primarily by dedicated matrix units
$131{,}072$ MACs ($256 \times 512$), executed primarily by vector units
$8{,}388{,}608$ MACs ($2 \times 32 \times 256 \times 512$), executed primarily by special function units
$16{,}384$ MACs ($32 \times 512$), executed primarily by scalar ALUs
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The total MAC count is $\text{batch\_size} \times d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}} = 32 \times 256 \times 512 = 4{,}194{,}304$ MACs (or $\approx 8.39$ MFLOPs when counting multiplies and additions separately). Because this computation is a dense many-to-many matrix multiplication, it maps directly to dedicated matrix units that execute block matrix multiplications in parallel. The choice of 131,072 MACs calculates the parameter count for a single sample rather than the full batch of 32. The SFU and scalar choices misassign the primitive and calculate incorrect operation counts.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the exact MAC count for a batched linear layer and identify the primary compute primitive responsible for its execution.

questions.question: In GPU SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) execution, what occurs when threads within the same 32-thread warp take diverging branches of a conditional statement (`if-else`)?
choices: The hardware serializes execution of both branches, executing each path with inactive thread lanes masked off, which reduces effective computational throughput
The warp dynamically splits across two independent streaming multiprocessors so both branch paths execute in parallel at full throughput
The GPU raises a hardware trap and falls back to CPU scalar execution to resolve the divergent branch
The threads execute simultaneously without penalty because each thread has an independent instruction fetch and decode pipeline
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Threads in a warp share a single instruction fetch and issue unit and execute in lock-step. When control flow diverges, the warp must execute the `if` path with non-taking threads masked, then execute the `else` path with taking threads masked. This serialization halves effective execution throughput for the divergent section. The claim that warps split across SMs misdescribes the hardware: warps never migrate across SMs mid-instruction. The CPU fallback claim is false. The independent instruction fetch claim describes MIMD, not SIMT.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the warp divergence penalty in GPU SIMT architectures and its impact on computational throughput.

questions.question: A $128 \times 128$ systolic array executes a large matrix multiplication. Explain quantitatively why its energy per multiply-accumulate (MAC) is dramatically lower than a traditional vector-unit implementation of the same operation.
questions.answer: In a $128 \times 128$ systolic array, each input and weight operand is loaded once from the array boundary and pulsed rhythmically through the 2D grid of processing elements on short nearest-neighbor wires. Each operand participates in 128 MAC operations before being discarded, amortizing a single memory fetch across 128 operations. A traditional vector unit must repeatedly read and write operands from register files or SRAM across long global wires for each operation. Because data movement over global wires and memory costs orders of magnitude more energy than arithmetic, amortizing memory traffic by $128\times$ translates directly into a proportional reduction in energy per MAC.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify how operand reuse and nearest-neighbor dataflow in systolic arrays minimize data movement energy relative to vector units.

questions.question: True or False: A 50-percent unstructured pruning pass delivers roughly the same inference speedup as a 2:4 structured-sparsity pass on modern tensor hardware, because both halve the number of nonzero multiply-accumulate operations.
questions.answer: False. Modern Sparse Tensor Cores support 2:4 structured sparsity with dedicated zero-skipping hardware and compact 2-bit index metadata per four-element block, delivering up to $2\times$ tensor-math throughput over dense execution. In contrast, unstructured pruning scatters zeros randomly, requiring heavy sparse-matrix indexing formats (like CSR) and creating irregular, uncoalesced memory accesses that destroy memory bandwidth and rarely translate to hardware speedup.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish structured N:M sparsity from unstructured sparsity in terms of hardware support and realizable speedup.

questions.question: A convolution layer produces 257 output channels and executes on a 128-wide tensor matrix unit. Two full tiles cover 256 channels, but the 257th channel forces a third tile. What fraction of the third tile's compute capacity is wasted, and what is the design implication?
choices: Exactly 50 percent is wasted because hardware automatically averages utilization across adjacent tiles
Zero percent is wasted because modern tensor cores dynamically shrink their physical execution width to match arbitrary odd dimensions

$127/128 \approx 99.2$ percent of the third tile is wasted; to avoid this 'fringe tax', model architects align layer channel and embedding dimensions to multiples of hardware tile widths (e.g., 128, 256)
$1/257 \approx 0.4$ percent is wasted because the cost is amortized across all output channels
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Physical tensor units have fixed hardware widths (128 lanes). When processing 257 channels, the first two tiles compute $2 \times 128 = 256$ channels at 100% utilization, while the third tile processes only 1 channel while 127 processing lanes sit idle—wasting $127/128 \approx 99.2\%$ of that tile's compute cycles. This underutilization penalty is the 'fringe tax', which is why production neural architectures select dimensions that are exact multiples of hardware tile sizes (such as 64, 128, 256, 512). The dynamic shrinkage claim contradicts physical silicon design.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the fringe-tax utilization loss from unaligned tensor dimensions on fixed-width matrix hardware.

questions.question: Why does Bfloat16 (BF16) format simplify mixed-precision neural network training compared to IEEE FP16, despite having fewer bits of precision in its mantissa?
choices: BF16 performs arithmetic twice as fast as FP16 because integer arithmetic units can execute it directly
BF16 uses an 8-bit exponent—the same as FP32—giving it the same dynamic range ($10^{-38}$ to $10^{38}$) and eliminating the underflow/overflow issues that require loss scaling in FP16
BF16 uses only 8 bits total per parameter, cutting memory bandwidth in half compared to 16-bit FP16
BF16 guarantees zero rounding error during gradient accumulation
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. FP16 has a 5-bit exponent and 10-bit mantissa, which provides high precision but a narrow dynamic range ($10^{-5}$ to $6.5 \times 10^4$), frequently causing gradients to underflow to zero unless explicit loss scaling is used. BF16 allocates 8 bits to the exponent and 7 bits to the mantissa, matching FP32's dynamic range and allowing seamless drop-in replacement for FP32 gradients and activations without loss scaling. The 8-bit total claim confuses BF16 with FP8. The integer-execution claim and zero-rounding-error claim are technically false.
questions.learning_objective: Compare BF16 and FP16 numerical representations in terms of dynamic range, precision trade-offs, and loss-scaling requirements.

questions.question: What structural mechanism enables a specialized Tensor Core instruction (such as `mma.sync`) to achieve multi-fold higher throughput than executing individual SIMD instructions for matrix multiplication?
choices: Tensor cores increase the clock frequency of the GPU by $10\times$ during matrix operations
Tensor cores eliminate the need for input tensors by computing matrix outputs analytically from random seeds
Tensor cores operate asynchronously without reading from or writing to any on-chip registers or memory

A single tensor instruction executes a full multi-dimensional matrix-multiply-accumulate tile directly in hardware, bypassing instruction fetch, decode, and issue overhead for dozens of separate scalar/vector operations while accumulating results in local registers
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. In standard SIMD/SIMT, computing a $16 \times 16$ matrix product requires fetching, decoding, issuing, and scheduling dozens of separate scalar or vector fused multiply-add (FMA) instructions, generating heavy instruction-pipeline and register-file traffic. A Tensor Core instruction exposes a hardware tile primitive (`mma.sync`) that executes the entire block matrix multiply in dedicated dense arithmetic datapaths in one logical operation, amortizing control overhead and keeping intermediate accumulators local. The clock-frequency claim is false. The analytical-seeds and no-registers claims are nonsensical.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how dedicated matrix hardware (Tensor Cores) amortizes instruction overhead and maximizes compute density.

questions.question: What is the central quantitative claim of the "AI memory wall" as the section frames it?
choices: Accelerators have too few arithmetic units to keep up with model demand, so the primary investment direction is adding more MAC units per chip
Compute throughput has scaled faster than memory bandwidth for multiple accelerator generations, so an increasing share of ML workload time and energy is spent moving data rather than computing on it
Adding HBM capacity automatically resolves memory-bound workloads by giving models more storage to work with
Only CPUs suffer from memory bottlenecks; accelerators avoid them architecturally by integrating compute and memory on one die
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The memory wall is a growth-rate gap: compute has scaled faster than bandwidth, so the ratio of bytes-per-FLOP the hardware can deliver shrinks each generation. The claim that more capacity fixes it inverts the bottleneck: bandwidth and latency, not total storage, are the binding constraints. The claim that only CPUs suffer contradicts the existence of HBM, NVLink, and on-chip scratchpads, which exist specifically because accelerators face the wall most acutely.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the AI memory wall as a compute-bandwidth growth-rate gap rather than a capacity gap.

questions.question: Why is on-chip SRAM indispensable on an accelerator that already has multi-TB/s HBM?
choices: HBM access takes tens to hundreds of nanoseconds of round-trip latency, too many cycles for arithmetic units to wait on directly; SRAM delivers operands at single-cycle latency, bridging the gap between HBM's bandwidth and the arithmetic units' cycle-scale demand
HBM cannot hold model parameters, so SRAM is needed to store weights that do not fit elsewhere
HBM is only used by CPUs and bypassed by accelerator kernels, which run entirely from SRAM
SRAM provides more total capacity than HBM, making it the correct tier for bulk storage
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The argument is about latency, not bandwidth: even a 2 TB/s HBM link cannot feed a MAC array that demands operands every cycle, because a round trip to HBM is already dozens of cycles. SRAM closes that latency gap by sitting physically next to the arithmetic units. The capacity claim inverts the hierarchy: HBM has more bytes, SRAM has faster bytes; they serve different roles precisely because they cannot replace one another.
questions.learning_objective: Justify why cycle-scale operand delivery requires on-chip memory even in the presence of high-bandwidth off-chip memory.

questions.question: Compare the memory-pressure profile that CNNs impose on an accelerator with the profile that large transformers impose, and explain how this comparison changes accelerator-selection priorities.
questions.answer: CNNs reuse small convolutional filters across many spatial positions, giving high operand-reuse ratios and letting tiled execution keep weights resident in on-chip SRAM; the binding constraint is compute throughput once the working set fits. Large transformers read billions of parameters with minimal reuse at batch 1 and add KV-cache growth that scales linearly with sequence length, so each decoded token pulls most of the model's weights across the memory hierarchy. The consequence for hardware selection is that CNN accelerators can lean on dense compute ratios and modest HBM, while transformer inference accelerators must prioritize HBM bandwidth, KV-cache-aware memory layouts, and interconnect bandwidth for sharded weights—making peak-FLOP/s benchmarks actively misleading for transformer deployment.
questions.learning_objective: Compare CNN and transformer memory-pressure profiles and derive the implications for accelerator-selection priorities.

questions.question: Order the following storage and communication tiers from fastest operand delivery (cycles) to slowest (hundreds of thousands of cycles or more) for an accelerator executing a tensor workload: (1) HBM device memory, (2) L2 or shared on-chip cache, (3) register file, (4) PCIe transfer from host memory.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (3) register file, (2) L2 or shared on-chip cache, (1) HBM device memory, (4) PCIe transfer from host memory. Registers deliver operands at the clock cycle; on-chip caches take tens of cycles; HBM costs hundreds of cycles; PCIe sits at the thinnest taper of the hierarchy at hundreds of thousands of cycles or more once queueing and protocol overhead are included. Swapping HBM and PCIe would ignore the bandwidth-taper argument the chapter develops—PCIe is one to two orders of magnitude slower than HBM and is precisely why host-to-device transfers often dominate end-to-end wall clock.
questions.learning_objective: Order the accelerator memory hierarchy by operand-delivery latency and justify why PCIe sits at the slowest end.

questions.question: An eight-GPU node uses NVLink between GPUs and multi-TB/s HBM per GPU. The team observes that their input pipeline spends most of its time transferring data from the host CPU rather than computing on the GPUs. Which link is most likely the bottleneck?
choices: The HBM interface, because device-local memory is structurally slower than host DRAM on modern systems
The NVLink fabric between GPUs, because inter-GPU links always represent the slowest communication tier in a node
The register file, because registers cannot sustain streaming input data for deep-learning batches
The PCIe host-device link, which is roughly one to two orders of magnitude slower than HBM and slower than NVLink, so host-fed pipelines often saturate PCIe before any on-device link is stressed
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The section's bandwidth-taper ordering puts PCIe at the narrow end: HBM >> NVLink >> PCIe, and once a pipeline is host-fed, PCIe becomes the binding link. The claim that HBM is slower than host DRAM inverts reality (HBM is roughly $10{-}50\times$ faster than typical DDR). The claim that NVLink is always slowest contradicts its design purpose as a high-bandwidth peer link. The register-file framing confuses tier with role: registers feed MAC units, not input pipelines.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the likely bottleneck link in a host-fed multi-GPU pipeline using the bandwidth-taper hierarchy.

questions.question: Which model family most strongly stresses memory capacity plus interconnect bandwidth rather than compute throughput at inference time?
choices: Small CNNs with tight spatial locality and filter reuse, which fit comfortably in on-chip buffers
Standard image-classification CNNs on moderate input resolutions, which achieve high arithmetic intensity
Large transformers with tens to hundreds of billions of parameters and linearly growing KV cache, where per-token work is dominated by reading weights across the hierarchy
Dense GEMM workloads at very large batch size, which amortize weight reads across many samples and become compute bound
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Transformer inference pulls most of the weight matrix per token at small batch and compounds that with KV-cache growth, putting the binding constraint on HBM bandwidth and, at large model sizes, on the interconnect that links sharded weights. The three other choices describe regimes the chapter explicitly identifies as compute-bound or reuse-friendly, so they do not match the capacity-plus-interconnect pressure profile.
questions.learning_objective: Classify which model family most strongly stresses memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth.

layer-level classification (dense, convolution, LayerNorm, softmax)
batching as a ridge-crossing mechanism
rising ridge points and regime shifts

questions.question: On an A100 with a ridge point of about 153 FLOP/byte, which statement correctly classifies whether a kernel is compute bound or memory bound?
choices: Classification depends on the parameter count of the model: larger models are always compute bound
Classification depends on whether the workload is training or inference, not on arithmetic intensity
Kernels with arithmetic intensity above about 153 FLOP/byte sit on the compute ceiling and are compute bound; kernels below that threshold sit on the bandwidth slope and are memory bound
Kernels are compute bound if they use tensor cores and memory bound otherwise, regardless of arithmetic intensity
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The ridge point is the arithmetic-intensity threshold where attainable performance switches from bandwidth-limited to compute-limited; a kernel's position relative to that threshold is what determines the regime. The parameter-count framing confuses capacity with intensity. The training-versus-inference framing ignores that the same operation can be on either side of the ridge depending on its FLOP-per-byte ratio. The tensor-core framing inverts cause and effect: using tensor cores raises the compute ceiling, but it does not determine which ceiling the workload sits under.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a kernel as compute bound or memory bound using its arithmetic intensity relative to the accelerator's ridge point.

questions.question: A dense linear layer at batch size 1 sits near 1 FLOP/byte on an A100 (ridge point about 153 FLOP/byte). At batch size 256 the same layer sits at roughly 205 FLOP/byte. Explain the mechanism that shifts the layer across the ridge and quantify which levers moved.
questions.answer: At batch size 1 each output coordinate reads one row of the weight matrix, does one dot product, and discards the weights — FLOP/byte is roughly $\mathcal{O}(1)$ because every weight is used once per byte loaded. At batch size 256 the same weight row is multiplied against 256 input vectors before being discarded, so weight reads are amortized across many outputs: total FLOPs grow $256\times$ while bytes moved grows only modestly because the weight matrix is still read once per tile. Crossing from about 1 FLOP/byte to about 205 FLOP/byte moves the layer past the A100's roughly 153 FLOP/byte ridge, so the bottleneck flips from HBM bandwidth to tensor-core compute. The practical implication: batching is the primary lever for converting a bandwidth-bound inference kernel into a compute-bound one.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify how increasing batch size raises arithmetic intensity and can move a kernel across the ridge point.

questions.question: Which operation is most likely to remain severely memory bound on an A100 even at large batch sizes?
choices: A large $3 \times 3$ convolution with 256 input and output channels and heavy spatial filter reuse
A large batched dense matrix multiplication using tensor cores at batch size 1024
A transformer QKV projection that shares input activations across the three projection matrices

LayerNorm, which performs on the order of a handful of arithmetic operations per activation element and reads the entire activation tensor to compute per-sample statistics across the feature dimension
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. LayerNorm has arithmetic intensity around 1 to 2 FLOP/byte — roughly two orders of magnitude below the A100's 153 FLOP/byte ridge — so no realistic batching or tiling can pull it across the ridge; the operation is structurally bandwidth bound. The convolution and QKV projection cases have enough reuse to approach or exceed the ridge once tiled and batched, and the large batched GEMM is the canonical compute-bound kernel on tensor cores.
questions.learning_objective: Identify a canonical low-intensity normalization operation that remains memory bound regardless of batching.

questions.question: True or False: Buying an H100 with higher peak FLOP/s than an A100 guarantees that every kernel compute-bound on the A100 stays compute-bound on the H100.
questions.answer: False. Newer accelerators raise peak FLOP/s faster than HBM bandwidth, which pushes the ridge point upward — the A100 sits near 153 FLOP/byte while the H100 sits near 295 FLOP/byte. A kernel with arithmetic intensity of 200 FLOP/byte is compute bound on the A100 but falls below the H100 ridge and becomes memory bound on the upgraded hardware, delivering less speedup than the peak-FLOP/s ratio would suggest.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize that rising ridge points on newer accelerators can convert compute-bound kernels into memory-bound ones.

questions.question: A team profiles a GPT-2 batch-1 decode kernel on an A100 and measures 0.8 FLOP/byte of weight and activation traffic against a 153 FLOP/byte ridge. Because the kernel sits roughly $190\times$ below the ____, the first productive optimizations reduce bytes moved through fusion, layout changes, or lower-precision weights, rather than adding more compute silicon.
questions.answer: ridge point. It is the hardware-specific arithmetic-intensity threshold at which the roofline transitions from the bandwidth slope to the compute ceiling; a kernel sitting far below that threshold cannot use added compute until its byte traffic is cut.
questions.learning_objective: Infer from a measured FLOP/byte ratio that a kernel sits far below the ridge point and select the appropriate optimization family.

questions.question: A team profiles GPT-2 autoregressive inference at batch 1 on an A100 and finds realized throughput below 1 percent of peak. Which optimization direction is most justified first?
choices: Reduce bytes moved per token through operator fusion, quantization of weights to INT8, or increasing batch size — each raises arithmetic intensity toward the ridge
Upgrade to a newer accelerator with $2\times$ the peak FLOP/s, because more compute throughput is the standard remedy for low utilization
Convert all operations to FP64 for better numerical stability, which will let the kernel stay on the compute ceiling longer
Replace tensor cores with scalar cores to better match the kernel's low observed utilization
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The 1-percent utilization signature plus batch-1 autoregressive decode is the canonical bandwidth-bound regime: each token pulls the full weight matrix for one dot product per parameter, so the kernel sits far below the ridge and gains come from cutting bytes moved. The newer-accelerator answer actually makes the problem worse because rising ridge points on newer chips demand higher intensity. The FP64 path doubles bytes moved and worsens the bottleneck. The scalar-core answer abandons the array parallelism that exists for exactly this workload shape.
questions.learning_objective: Select the optimization family matching a batch-1 autoregressive-decode profile with bandwidth-bound signature.

joint coupling of placement and memory allocation
loop ordering as a data-reuse lever
combinatorial explosion and the need for structured strategies

questions.question: Which decomposition best captures the three dimensions of hardware mapping for neural-network execution?
choices: Choosing the programming language and framework that will implement the model at deployment time
Operation placement on specific compute resources, tensor allocation across levels of the memory hierarchy, and temporal execution order with synchronization—all decided jointly
Randomly distributing tensor operations across available cores to achieve fair load balancing
Pruning or quantizing the model so fewer parameters need to be stored on the accelerator
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Mapping binds a logical computation to physical resources along three axes: where computation runs, where data lives, and when each piece executes. The language-choice framing confuses deployment tooling with hardware mapping. The random-distribution claim omits locality, which is the central concern. The pruning claim describes an algorithmic compression step, not hardware mapping.
questions.learning_objective: Classify placement, memory allocation, and execution order as the three joint dimensions of hardware mapping for a neural-network workload.

questions.question: Explain why computation placement and memory allocation must be decided jointly rather than independently, using a concrete example of how decoupling them degrades performance.
questions.answer: Placement decides which processing element runs a kernel, and allocation decides which tier of the memory hierarchy holds its operands; neither decision is meaningful without the other, because operand-delivery latency is a function of both. Consider a kernel placed on a fast PE whose operand tensors were allocated to off-chip HBM: the PE idles on every access because HBM latency is tens to hundreds of cycles, so the hardware choice is wasted. Conversely, operands in on-chip SRAM bound to a distant PE still incur traversal cost across the on-chip network. The system consequence is that mapping must co-optimize both axes to close the latency gap between where compute happens and where data lives—a point that becomes central to dataflow-strategy selection in the next section.
questions.learning_objective: Justify the joint-optimization coupling between operation placement and memory allocation using the operand-delivery-latency mechanism.

questions.question: A 2D convolution has loops over output-height, output-width, input-channels, output-channels, filter-height, and filter-width. Why does reordering these loops materially affect performance even though the arithmetic result is identical?
choices: Loop order determines the mathematical value of the convolution, so different orders produce different numerical outputs
Loop order only affects code readability and has no effect on runtime performance on modern hardware
The hardware accepts exactly one legal loop nesting per convolution kernel, so reordering is impossible rather than inefficient

Loop order determines which variables become the innermost (fastest-changing) indices, which in turn controls which operands can be reused from a register or cache versus reloaded from a slower tier—turning a high-reuse schedule into a schedule that reloads the same data repeatedly
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Loop ordering is semantically identity-preserving but changes the reuse footprint: putting output-channels as the innermost loop keeps one filter resident across many MACs; putting input-channels innermost forces the accumulator to live in a register while different weights stream past. The mathematical-result claim is false for associative accumulation. The readability-only claim misses the central lesson. The one-legal-nesting claim contradicts the entire compiler-scheduling discussion.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how loop ordering changes operand reuse and memory traffic without changing a kernel's semantics.

questions.question: A team profiles a transformer kernel and finds that its activations are allocated to HBM while the kernel is placed on a PE cluster with large L2 capacity and strong peer bandwidth. HBM utilization saturates at 95 percent while PE utilization sits at 18 percent. Which mapping decision failed?
choices: Operation placement: the PE cluster is too fast for this kernel, so moving the operation onto a slower cluster would improve apparent utilization
Memory allocation: the activations should have been tiled and staged into L2 so their reuse across attention heads is served by the fast tier rather than pulled from HBM every access
Execution order: serializing attention heads would reduce HBM pressure by limiting concurrent accesses
Precision choice: switching from FP16 to FP32 would let the kernel use more of the available HBM bandwidth
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. It names the allocation failure: placement was reasonable, but activations were not staged into the fast tier that would serve their reuse pattern, so the PEs starve on HBM reads (95 percent saturation) while arithmetic capacity runs at 18 percent. The placement-too-fast answer inverts the diagnosis: the bottleneck is HBM, not PE capacity. Serializing heads reduces concurrency but does not fix the allocation; the same bytes still traverse HBM. Raising precision doubles the byte traffic and makes the bottleneck worse.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose a mapping failure by identifying whether placement, memory allocation, or execution order was misconfigured given a saturated-HBM profile.

questions.question: Why is brute-force search over all legal mappings impractical even for a single layer?
choices: Modern compilers already know the optimal mapping analytically for every accelerator, so search is unnecessary
Only graph neural networks have enough operator complexity to make the search space nontrivial

The number of legal loop permutations, parallelization decompositions, and memory-placement choices grows combinatorially, so the legal-mapping space for a single convolution can exceed billions of candidates—well beyond any exhaustive evaluation
Legal mappings number in the low dozens for typical kernels, so search completes in milliseconds
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Loop-ordering permutations, tile-size choices, parallel-axis decompositions, and memory-level placement multiply into a space that is factorial in some axes and exponential in others, pushing the candidate count far past any exhaustive budget. The compiler-knows-analytically claim contradicts the existence of autotuners and cost models. The GNN-only claim misattributes the problem to a specific architecture; dense convolutions alone produce the combinatorial explosion. The claim of low dozens contradicts the chapter's combinatorial analysis.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why accelerator mapping requires heuristics or structured strategies rather than exhaustive search.

tensor layout and hardware access-pattern alignment

tiling for fit-and-reuse in fast memory
hybrid mapping across architecture-specific reuse patterns
rationale.question_strategy: Cover the three stationary strategies against a reuse pattern, connect layout choices to hardware memory-access preferences, quantify fusion's memory-traffic benefit, probe tiling's purpose, and close with a hybrid-mapping scenario.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Starts with dataflow-to-reuse matching, moves to layout-and-access-pattern reasoning, quantifies fusion benefits, tests tiling motivation, and ends with a hybrid mapping scenario.

rationale.ranking_explanation: Operationalizes the chapter's memory-centric worldview and directly addresses a listed learning objective; warrants a full quiz.

questions.question: A CNN uses $3\times 3$ filters reused across thousands of spatial positions per input image. Which stationary dataflow best matches this reuse profile?
choices: Weight-stationary, because filter weights are read once at the array edge and reused across every spatial application while activations stream through
Output-stationary, because CNNs generate more output positions than the hardware can accumulate in place
Input-stationary, because filters are too large to fit in local memory and must stream in from DRAM
No stationary choice matters because dataflow has no effect on memory traffic once arithmetic is executed
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The CNN reuse pattern—same small filter, many spatial applications—is exactly the case weight-stationary was designed for: keep filter weights in the local tier and stream activations past them. The output-stationary framing inverts which operand is reused; it matches layers where partial sums accumulate over many input contractions, not layers where the same weights apply across many outputs. The input-stationary claim misreads the size asymmetry (filters are the small operand). The claim of no effect contradicts the chapter's central argument.
questions.learning_objective: Select a stationary dataflow strategy by matching it to a workload's operand-reuse pattern.

questions.question: A GPU team is deciding between NHWC and NCHW tensor layout for a convolution-heavy inference pipeline. Why can channels-last NHWC be preferred for the forward pass on modern GPU kernels?
choices: NHWC places values from the same spatial position but different channels at contiguous addresses, so hardware processing adjacent channels for one pixel can read memory efficiently in a single block rather than scattered reads
NHWC maximizes branch-prediction efficiency, which dominates convolution performance on GPUs
NHWC is the universally fastest layout on CPUs, so GPU engineers inherit the convention
NHWC eliminates the need for any tensor layout transformations in any framework
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Contiguous memory access—parallel compute units reading contiguous addresses in one operation—is a core hardware preference, and channels-last layout makes adjacent-channel accesses contiguous for kernels that vectorize across channels. The branch-prediction framing imports a CPU-centric concern that is minor on GPUs. The CPU-always-faster claim is false; CPU preferences depend on the kernel and cache geometry. The no-transformations claim contradicts the need for framework compilation passes to match different hardware preferences.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why channels-last tensor layout can align with hardware memory-access preferences to improve convolution throughput.

questions.question: Fusing Conv2D, BatchNorm, and ReLU into a single kernel does not change the total floating-point operation count. Explain quantitatively why fusion can still double or triple throughput on a bandwidth-bound inference segment.
questions.answer: Unfused, each operator writes its output tensor to HBM and the next operator reads it back, so three operators move the activation tensor six times through HBM (three writes plus three reads). Fusion keeps the intermediate activation resident in registers or on-chip SRAM across the three stages, cutting the HBM traffic for that segment from six tensor traversals to two (one input read plus one output write). On a bandwidth-bound segment with arithmetic intensity well below the ridge, wall-clock time is proportional to bytes moved, so cutting bytes by roughly $3\times$ yields a proportional speedup. The system consequence: fusion is the primary compiler lever for bandwidth-bound model segments and is most effective precisely where the arithmetic intensity is lowest.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the memory-traffic reduction delivered by operator fusion on a bandwidth-bound segment and relate it to realized speedup.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of tiling in accelerator execution?
choices: To change the numerical order of operations enough that the final result becomes slightly more accurate
To eliminate parallelism by serializing work into smaller sequential pieces that are easier to schedule

To partition a large tensor computation into blocks sized for fast local memory so each block's operands can be reused many times before eviction, raising arithmetic intensity by reducing redundant traffic from slower memory tiers
To guarantee that every operation becomes compute bound regardless of its underlying arithmetic intensity
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Tiling shapes work to fit in fast memory so operands are reused intensively before being evicted; the reused operands do not need to be re-fetched from slow memory, which directly raises arithmetic intensity. The accuracy claim confuses tiling with mixed-precision accumulation. The serialization claim inverts the purpose: tiles are precisely the unit of parallel execution on arrays. The compute-bound guarantee is false; tiling can shift the operating point on the roofline but cannot change a kernel's structural intensity.
questions.learning_objective: Explain tiling as a locality-optimizing partitioning that raises arithmetic intensity by fitting working sets into fast memory.

questions.question: True or False: A single stationary dataflow is optimal across CNNs, transformers, and MLPs, so hybrid mapping is mostly implementation overhead without real performance benefit.
questions.answer: False. CNNs reuse small filters across spatial positions and favor weight-stationary; attention blocks stress bandwidth through large KV reads and favor cache-aware or output-staging strategies; MLP blocks look like large GEMMs and prefer blocked weight-reuse with fusion. Each reuse pattern is different enough that forcing one strategy on all can leave performance on the table, which is why production compilers and runtimes implement hybrid mapping.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize that layer-class reuse-pattern diversity makes hybrid mapping a real performance lever rather than implementation overhead.

questions.question: A compiler maps a transformer composed of attention blocks and MLP layers onto an A100. Which mapping strategy best matches the section's argument?
choices: Use the same weight-stationary scheme for every layer because consistency across the graph is more important than per-layer locality

Use memory-aware attention kernels (fused softmax and masking with on-chip tiling) for attention blocks while using blocked GEMM-style tiling with operator fusion for MLP layers—matching each layer class to the dataflow that serves its reuse pattern
Prefer row-major layouts uniformly because they are cache-friendly on CPUs, regardless of the target accelerator
Disable fusion and tiling globally so runtime decisions remain maximally flexible
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Attention and MLP stress different reuse patterns—attention has KV-cache reads with limited weight reuse, while MLPs look like large GEMMs with heavy weight reuse—so the dominant bottlenecks differ and so should the dataflow strategy. The uniform-weight-stationary answer sacrifices attention performance for simplicity. The row-major-CPU answer imports the wrong hardware's convention. The disable-all answer forfeits the two largest optimization levers the chapter has identified.
questions.learning_objective: Design a layer-aware hybrid mapping strategy for a transformer by matching attention and MLP layers to their best dataflow.

boundary between compile-time plans and runtime adaptation

questions.question: Why do ML compilers need different optimization priorities from traditional compilers?
choices: ML programs no longer require any memory management, so compilers can skip allocation and placement entirely
Traditional compilers already optimize GPUs and TPUs perfectly, so ML compilers exist only to provide a friendlier API
ML models are too small for instruction-level optimization to matter, so any compiler will produce equivalent code

ML programs are tensor-level computation graphs, so the dominant optimization axes are graph transformations (fusion, layout, partitioning), memory-traffic planning, and accelerator-specific execution—not instruction-level optimizations on sequential scalar code
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The optimization axis shift from instruction stream to tensor graph is the core reason ML compilers diverge: fusion, layout, and partitioning have no counterpart in a C compiler. The claim that memory management disappears is the opposite of the truth; tensor placement and movement are central. The claim that traditional compilers already optimize GPUs ignores that vendor stacks exist precisely because generic compilers cannot target accelerator pipelines. The small-models claim contradicts the existence of frontier training jobs.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the optimization axes of ML compilers with those of traditional compilers.

questions.question: Order the following ML compilation stages by their causal dependencies: (1) graph optimization rewrites the computation graph (fusion, layout), (2) kernel selection picks a concrete implementation (cuBLAS, cuDNN, handwritten) for each operator, (3) memory planning assigns tensor buffers to hierarchy tiers, (4) computation scheduling fixes the temporal execution order across resources, (5) code generation emits device-specific machine code.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (1) graph optimization rewrites the computation graph, (2) kernel selection picks a concrete implementation for each operator, (3) memory planning assigns tensor buffers to hierarchy tiers, (4) computation scheduling fixes the temporal execution order, (5) code generation emits device-specific machine code. Each stage has a data dependency on the prior one: the compiler cannot choose kernels for operators until fusion has settled the graph; it cannot plan memory until kernel choice reveals working-set sizes; it cannot schedule before memory placement is known; it cannot emit code before the schedule is fixed. Swapping scheduling ahead of memory planning forces the scheduler to reason about access costs it does not yet know—the same mistake early ML compilers made before adopting this pipeline.
questions.learning_objective: Order the causal dependencies among the five ML compilation stages and justify why reordering them breaks the pipeline.

questions.question: A model runs $4\times$ faster under an optimizing backend than in eager execution while the model architecture is unchanged. Explain which compiler transformations are most likely responsible and why they deliver the gain without touching the model's math.
questions.answer: Four transformations explain the observed $4\times$ result. First, operator fusion collapses adjacent kernels (Conv-BN-ReLU or softmax-masking-matmul) into a single launch, cutting kernel-launch overhead and intermediate HBM traffic. Second, kernel selection substitutes vendor-optimized implementations (cuDNN, cuBLAS) for the generic reference path. Third, layout transformation permutes tensor memory order to enable coalesced access on the target accelerator. Fourth, memory planning folds buffers onto reused allocations, eliminating redundant transfers. None changes the model's arithmetic output; all change the bytes-moved and launch-cost profile.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how compiler transformations deliver multi-x speedups without changing model semantics, naming the specific transforms involved.

questions.question: What is the main goal of graph optimization before hardware-specific code generation?
choices: Bind every operation permanently to a fixed physical core, ignoring later scheduling or runtime adaptation

Rewrite the computation graph to eliminate redundant operations, fuse adjacent kernels, adjust tensor layouts, and reduce intermediate activations before committing to kernel and placement choices that depend on the final graph structure
Convert all arithmetic to FP64 for numerical accuracy regardless of the target hardware's capabilities
Replace vendor-optimized libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN) with generic scalar implementations for portability
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Graph optimization is the high-level restructuring stage: rewrite the graph into a form the downstream stages can compile efficiently. The core-binding answer overreaches into placement and scheduling decisions that happen after graph optimization. The FP64 answer inverts the trend toward reduced precision. The generic-libraries answer describes the opposite of what graph optimization aims at: vendor libraries are the target of kernel selection, not competition.
questions.learning_objective: Describe the role of graph optimization as the high-level restructuring stage that precedes kernel and placement commitments.

questions.question: A compiler lowers the same GEMM into code for an A100, a TPU, and a CPU inference server. Why is kernel selection not a trivial library lookup?
choices: The same abstract GEMM has many concrete implementations whose best choice varies with matrix shape, precision, batch size, and current hardware state; a cuBLAS call that wins at $4096\times 4096$ FP16 may lose at $128\times 128$ FP32, so the compiler must choose among implementations using cost models or profiling
Accelerators execute only one kernel type for the entire model, so kernel selection collapses to a single per-hardware choice
Kernel choice is unrelated to tensor shape or memory bandwidth, so a fixed library call suffices in every case
Vendors do not provide optimized kernel libraries for ML workloads, so all kernels must be generated from scratch
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Shape, precision, and batch regime each pick different winning implementations, which is why cost models and autotuners exist. The single-kernel-per-chip claim contradicts the existence of per-operator implementations in every production stack. The shape-and-bandwidth-unrelated claim denies the roofline framing the chapter developed. The no-libraries claim contradicts cuBLAS, cuDNN, oneDNN, and XLA—the entire ecosystem kernel selection chooses among.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why kernel selection depends on workload shape, precision, and hardware state rather than a fixed library lookup.

questions.question: True or False: A complete compile-time execution plan is sufficient by itself, so runtime systems function as little more than administrative wrappers around compiled binaries.
questions.answer: False. Compile-time plans assume fixed conditions—batch shape, memory state, no contention—that production workloads violate routinely. Runtime systems adapt to variable batch sizes, fragmenting device memory, multi-tenant interference, and thermal throttling, and they can override compile-time kernel choices when hardware state changes. The compile-then-run boundary is a handoff, not a closure.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish compile-time plan generation from runtime adaptation and identify what compile-time planning cannot capture.

questions.question: Why do AI systems need specialized runtime support even after a model has been fully compiled?
choices: Compilation cannot produce executable machine code for accelerators, so a runtime is required to translate the plan into instructions
Runtimes exist only to provide a user interface for monitoring accelerator temperatures and utilization
Compiled execution plans are mathematically incomplete and produce wrong results without runtime correction

Production conditions—variable batch size, memory fragmentation, multi-tenant contention, thermal throttling—routinely diverge from the fixed assumptions baked into compile-time plans, so execution must adapt to actual state rather than follow a static script
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The runtime adapts to exactly the conditions compile-time cannot see: dynamic shapes, memory state, contention, and hardware state. The claim that compilation cannot produce code contradicts the existence of every AOT-compiled binary. The UI-only framing trivializes the runtime's scheduling and kernel-selection responsibilities. The mathematically-incomplete claim confuses correctness with adaptation; compiled plans are correct under their assumptions but suboptimal when conditions change.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why runtime systems are required even when compile-time optimization has already occurred.

questions.question: A transformer inference service receives requests with sequence lengths ranging from 64 to 8192 tokens. Explain how runtime dynamic kernel execution improves performance compared to a single compile-time plan built for an average sequence length.
questions.answer: A single compiled plan picks one tile size, one memory layout, and one kernel variant optimized for a fixed assumed shape, so it under-utilizes the accelerator on short sequences (too much reserved KV-cache and launch overhead per token) and overruns memory or slows catastrophically on long sequences (tile too small, forcing many launches). A dynamic runtime measures the actual shape at request time and selects among pre-compiled kernel variants or rebuilds tile parameters: short requests use a compact kernel with low launch overhead, long requests use a larger tiled kernel with staged KV-cache. The consequence is that realized latency tracks each request's inherent cost rather than the average case, so p99 latency and mean utilization both improve.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how runtime kernel adaptation reduces per-request latency variance for variable-shape inference workloads.

questions.question: A runtime observes a batch shape that would benefit from FP16 tensor cores and replaces a compiler-selected FP32 matrix kernel with an FP16 tensor-core kernel for that step. Which justification best matches the section's argument?
choices: The runtime swaps kernels only to reduce accuracy for easier debugging, never for performance
Compiled kernels are unexecutable on real hardware until the runtime rewrites the entire graph

Runtime kernel selection can exploit actual hardware state and workload shape: if current conditions permit reduced precision (precision budget, tensor-core availability, input range), the runtime substitutes a faster implementation that the compile-time plan conservatively rejected
FP16 tensor-core substitution is a CPU-only optimization and has no effect on accelerators
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. It names the actual mechanism: the runtime has information the compiler lacked—current shape, current precision budget, current tensor-core availability—and exercises a pre-authorized alternate path when that information favors a faster kernel. The accuracy-for-debugging claim reverses the motivation. The claim that kernels are unexecutable contradicts standard AOT deployment. The CPU-only claim contradicts production inference stacks.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why runtime kernel selection may override compile-time choices by leveraging information unavailable at compile time.

questions.question: True or False: An inference service that benchmarks at a stable 10 ms p99 latency in isolation will deliver roughly the same p99 under multi-tenant production load because the compiled execution plan and the hardware are unchanged.
questions.answer: False. Multi-tenant production introduces HBM bandwidth contention, L2 cache pollution from neighboring kernels, and thermal headroom changes that can raise p99 latency materially relative to an isolated benchmark—even with the identical compiled plan on identical silicon. The runtime's ability to detect and react to these conditions is exactly the adaptation the section motivates.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish stable-benchmark performance from multi-tenant production behavior using specific contention mechanisms.

questions.question: What is the main role of kernel scheduling inside the AI runtime?
choices: Rewrite the model architecture to reduce parameter count before execution begins
Write training checkpoints to SSD at fixed intervals during inference
Determine when and where selected kernels execute on available resources so compute, data movement, and host-device transfers are overlapped and accelerators stay continuously fed
Guarantee identical wall-clock latency for every kernel, regardless of operand shape or resource contention
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Scheduling exists to keep the accelerator's arithmetic, memory, and host-device paths all working in parallel so no resource idles while another waits. The model-rewriting answer describes graph optimization, which is a compiler role. The checkpoint answer is unrelated to inference scheduling. The identical-latency guarantee is physically impossible because kernels differ in shape, dependencies, and resource demand.
questions.learning_objective: Describe the runtime scheduler's role in overlapping compute and data movement to sustain accelerator utilization.

multi-chip and wafer-scale approaches

fault tolerance as a first-class concern at scale

rationale.difficulty_progression: Begins with a communication-overhead diagnosis, moves to approaches that minimize inter-chip cost, analyzes coherence costs at scale, and closes with a hardened fault-tolerance scenario.
rationale.integration: Connects prior material on all-reduce, communication tax, and distributed training to the accelerator chapter's hardware perspective.

questions.question: A training run scales from 8 to 64 accelerators and sees only a $5.2\times$ speedup rather than $8\times$. Which factor best explains the diminishing return?
choices: Accelerators lose arithmetic capability when connected together through NVLink or Ethernet, so per-device throughput drops as the cluster grows
Memory capacity decreases as more accelerators are added, forcing smaller batches that scale worse
All-reduce removes the need for per-device computation once two or more devices are present

Gradient synchronization, parameter broadcast, and inter-node coordination create communication overhead that can grow as more devices participate in every all-reduce, reducing parallel efficiency despite added compute
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Communication and coordination grow with device count, reducing parallel efficiency; the observed $5.2\times$ rather than $8\times$ speedup is evidence of that overhead. The claim that accelerators lose arithmetic capability has no hardware basis. The capacity-decreases claim inverts the effect of adding devices. The all-reduce-removes-computation claim describes the opposite of what all-reduce does.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how communication overhead reduces parallel efficiency and limits multi-accelerator scaling.

questions.question: Which scaling approach most directly reduces inter-chip communication overhead by treating an entire wafer as one compute fabric?
choices: Wafer-scale integration, which keeps communication on a single large silicon die and avoids package boundaries, PCIe links, and network switches for most cross-compute-unit traffic
Chiplet packaging across standard CPU sockets, which routes most communication through motherboard interconnect
A conventional PCIe-attached multi-GPU workstation, which uses the host PCIe bus for inter-GPU traffic
A cluster linked only by commodity Ethernet, which amortizes communication across TCP/IP
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Wafer-scale integration eliminates the package-and-board traversal that dominates cross-chip latency, keeping most communication on-die. Chiplets still cross package boundaries. PCIe-attached multi-GPU workstations move cross-GPU traffic through PCIe, the slowest tier in the taper. Ethernet-only clusters add network-stack overhead on top of the physical link.
questions.learning_objective: Identify wafer-scale integration as the approach that most aggressively minimizes inter-chip communication overhead.

questions.question: Explain why memory coherence becomes a materially harder problem on multi-chip AI systems than on single-chip accelerators, and give one concrete consequence for parallelism design.
questions.answer: On a single die, cache coherence is managed by on-chip protocols operating at nanosecond latencies. Once many chips must share a consistent view of weights, gradients, or activations, coherence traffic must traverse package boundaries and interconnect fabric, each access costing hundreds to thousands of cycles and consuming coordination bandwidth that competes with useful data. In practice this drives distributed-training systems to replace shared-memory assumptions with explicit memory management where programmers control data placement and synchronization manually. The consequence is that multi-chip AI systems trade the programming convenience of shared memory for the predictability of explicit communication-aware parallelism.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why coherence costs grow superlinearly in multi-chip AI systems and justify the shift to explicit communication-aware parallelism.

questions.question: A team scales a training cluster from 64 to 4,096 GPUs. Which factor grows sharply and forces fault tolerance into the design's first-class concerns?
choices: Software-stack complexity grows but hardware failure rates stay negligible, so fault tolerance is still optional

Component mean-time-to-failure is roughly constant per GPU, so aggregate failure rate scales linearly with device count; at 4,096 GPUs a single failure that would lose 15 minutes of progress at 64 devices now occurs many times per day, requiring checkpointing and automatic recovery
Network topology becomes irrelevant at scale because all-reduce self-adapts to any shape
Thermal and power limits disappear at scale because heat dissipates across a larger footprint
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The aggregation effect dictates that per-device reliability is fixed, so fleet failure frequency scales with device count; a weekly failure at 64 devices becomes one about every few hours at 4,096. The software-complexity-only claim ignores hardware-induced failure frequency. The topology-irrelevant claim contradicts network scaling principles. The thermal-disappears claim inverts the physics: larger systems face more aggregate heat, not less.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the quantitative growth of failure frequency with device count and justify fault tolerance as a first-class concern at scale.

software orchestration complexity
